items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener
items.passage: Discovered in 1833 in a burial mound in northeastern Wales, the Mold cape is a masterpiece of prehistoric goldwork. Its maker began with a single gold ______ into a thin sheet and painstakingly embossed with ribs and bosses that imitate strings of beads, the cape would have restricted its wearer’s arm movements, suggesting a ceremonial purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence ends with “Its maker began with a single gold ingot.” The third sentence opens with the participial phrase “Hammered into a thin sheet and painstakingly embossed with ribs and bosses that imitate strings of beads,” which describes its subject, “the cape,” and then gives the main verb “would have restricted.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “hammered into a thin sheet ...” describe the ingot inside the second sentence, so the main clause “the cape would have restricted its wearer’s arm movements” is then joined to the main clause “Its maker began with a single gold ingot” with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “a single gold ingot hammered into a thin sheet ...” keeps the phrase in the second sentence, and the main clause “the cape would have restricted ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “That” begins a relative clause about the ingot that never gets its own verb: after the phrase “hammered into a thin sheet ...,” the sentence goes on with a new subject, “the cape,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Mold cape, Bronze Age gold cape found in 1833 in a burial mound at Mold, Flintshire, northeastern Wales; made from one gold ingot beaten thin, decorated with ribs and bosses like strings of beads; it would have restricted upper-arm movement, hence ceremonial). Known facts, no names. Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener of 16 words, a past participle with a relative clause that reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (a single gold ingot hammered into a thin sheet ...); cue outside a 6-word window (the splice shows at “the cape would have restricted,” 17 words after the blank); run 37 words; reasoning steps 3. Menu of a872c60a. No logic-wrong distractor (none in the template's band-7 models).
band7_moves: opener of 16 words, a past participle that reads naturally as a description of clause 1's last noun (a single gold ingot hammered into a thin sheet)
comma, glued and that options hold until the splice at “the cape would have restricted,” 17 words after the blank

band7.why: 16-word past-participle opener reads naturally on clause 1's last noun (a single gold ingot hammered into a thin sheet ...); comma, glued and that options all hold until the splice 17 words past the blank; a872c60a menu

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long noun-phrase opener
items.passage: Among the richest sources on Maya life under Spanish colonial rule are the Books of Chilam ______ of prophecies, chronicles, calendars, and medical remedies written down by Yucatec Maya scribes in the Latin alphabet, these manuscripts are named for a jaguar priest said to have foretold the arrival of foreigners.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “the Books of Chilam Balam.” The second sentence opens with the noun phrase “Collections of prophecies, chronicles, calendars, and medical remedies written down by Yucatec Maya scribes in the Latin alphabet,” which describes its subject, “these manuscripts,” and then gives the main verb “are named.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma makes “collections of prophecies ...” an appositive describing the Books of Chilam Balam in the first sentence, so the main clause “these manuscripts are named for a jaguar priest ...” is joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “Chilam Balam collections of prophecies” runs the title into the noun phrase, and the main clause “these manuscripts are named ...” then follows the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” joins “collections of prophecies ...” to “the Books of Chilam Balam” as a second subject of “are,” so the main clause “these manuscripts are named ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: literature and history (Books of Chilam Balam, Yucatec Maya manuscripts of the colonial period in Latin script; named for the jaguar priest, or prophet, Chilam Balam, said to have foretold the arrival of the Spanish). Known facts. Band-7 checks: opener of 17 words, an article-less noun-phrase appositive with its own series commas that reads as a description of the book title (940ff6f7 shape); clause 1 is inverted so its subject ends the clause; cue outside a 6-word window (splice at “these manuscripts are named,” 18 words after the blank); run 50 words; reasoning steps 3. Different opener type from w5b3_01 (noun phrase vs past participle).
band7_moves: opener of 17 words, an article-less noun-phrase appositive that reads as a description of clause 1's last noun (the Books of Chilam Balam, collections of ...)
comma, glued and and options hold until the splice at “these manuscripts are named,” 18 words after the blank
inverted clause 1 (Among ... are the Books of Chilam Balam) so the boundary falls right after its subject

band7.why: 17-word article-less noun-phrase opener with its own series reads as an appositive to the Books of Chilam Balam (940ff6f7 shape); splice shows 18 words later; inverted clause 1

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a prepositional opener
items.passage: Chemical gardens are plantlike mineral structures that chemists have documented since the 1600s. They form when crystals of a metal salt are submerged in a solution of sodium ______ the course of several minutes, each crystal sprouts hollow tubes that lengthen as water, drawn in by osmosis, repeatedly ruptures their delicate membranes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence ends with “submerged in a solution of sodium silicate.” The third sentence opens with the introductory phrase “Over the course of several minutes,” followed by its subject, “each crystal,” and its verb, “sprouts.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “each crystal sprouts hollow tubes ...” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice; the time phrase “over the course of several minutes” does not change that.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “submerged in a solution of sodium silicate over the course of several minutes” attaches the time phrase to the second sentence, and the main clause “each crystal sprouts ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “Which over the course of several minutes” begins a relative clause that never gets its own verb before the new subject “each crystal,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (chemical gardens: metal-salt crystals in sodium silicate, or water glass, grow hollow tubes as osmotic inflow repeatedly ruptures a silicate membrane; described by Glauber in the seventeenth century). Known chemistry, no names. Band-6 shape (2.10, 67667d72): a 6-word prepositional opener; the glued reading (submerged ... over the course of several minutes) is natural, and the splice appears at “each crystal sprouts,” 7 words after the blank. Run 38 words. No band-7 move intended.

band7.why: 6-word prepositional opener that glues naturally to clause 1, splice 7 words past the blank; 67667d72 band-6 shape, no band-7 move intended

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, contrast with the previous sentence
items.passage: An avatar, the character that represents a user in a virtual world, might seem like little more than a costume. Its appearance can shape how the user behaves ______ in a 2007 experiment, participants given taller avatars bargained more aggressively than participants given shorter ones, an example of what is now called the Proteus effect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adverb “though” belongs to the first clause: the claim that an avatar’s appearance “can shape how the user behaves” is the contrast with the previous sentence, in which an avatar “might seem like little more than a costume.” A comma sets “though” off from that clause, and a semicolon joins it to the next main clause, “participants given taller avatars bargained more aggressively than participants given shorter ones,” which gives evidence for that claim.

A.recipe: semicolon with a non-clause; logic-wrong adverb placement
A.why_wrong: Placing “though” after the semicolon turns what follows into a dependent clause, and a semicolon cannot join a main clause to a dependent clause. It would also wrongly present the 2007 experiment as a contrast with the claim it supports.

C.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “though” leave the two main clauses, “Its appearance can shape how the user behaves” and “participants given taller avatars bargained more aggressively ...,” joined by only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark after “though,” the word becomes a conjunction that presents the experiment as a concession, as if users of taller avatars bargaining more aggressively were at odds with the claim that an avatar’s appearance can shape behavior. The experiment supports that claim, so the contrast belongs with the previous sentence instead.

items.notes: Subject: social science (the Proteus effect: in a 2007 experiment by Nick Yee and Jeremy Bailenson, participants given taller avatars negotiated more aggressively than those given shorter ones; the researchers are not named in the passage). Review replaced the Lindy effect draft: official Words in Context item b92c13fa is about Taleb's idea that a nonperishable thing's age predicts its remaining life. Band-7 checks: the adverb closes clause 1, which reverses the previous sentence (little more than a costume vs shapes behavior); clause 2 is evidence for clause 1 with the same polarity, so the textbook placement (; though) and the subordinator reading (, though) fail only on meaning (logic-wrong A and D, as in CB's rationales for 21e58a83 and 5aa171de); clause 1 is a positive claim, so no 'but' or qualifying reading of ', though' can fit; menu of 21e58a83 and 5aa171de; run 35 words; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence (an avatar as little more than a costume vs an avatar that shapes behavior)
two logic-wrong distractors: “; though” (textbook side, also a semicolon before a dependent clause) and “, though” read as a subordinator, both failing because clause 2 supports clause 1
clause 2 opens with a time phrase before its subject and closes with a sentence appositive

band7.why: adverb closes clause 1 against the previous sentence; two logic-wrong distractors (; though and , though) that fail only because clause 2 supports clause 1, as in 21e58a83 and 5aa171de; no option is killed by one local fact

fixes: replaced the subject: the Lindy effect is the subject of official Words in Context item b92c13fa (Taleb, nonperishable entities); new subject the Proteus effect (grepped, claimed), same S1_adverb menu and key B

rebuilt clause 1 as a positive claim and clause 2 as same-polarity evidence, so neither “; though” (also a semicolon before a dependent clause) nor “, though” (concession) is defensible; the old “appear to ... according to a principle” wording allowed a hedging reading of “though”

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive: descriptor and title before a name that is followed by its verb
items.passage: Some chemical reactions arrange their own products into strikingly regular patterns. In 1896, German ______ observed that a drop of silver nitrate placed on a thin layer of gelatin containing potassium dichromate produced not a single smudge of precipitate but a series of concentric rings, a pattern now known as Liesegang rings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “German chemist” is a title placed directly before the name “Raphael Liesegang,” with no article, so the name is essential to identifying who is meant and is not set off with commas. The whole phrase “German chemist Raphael Liesegang” is the subject of the verb “observed,” and no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the title “German chemist” from the name it identifies; the name is restrictive here, so no comma belongs between them.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Liesegang” separates the subject “German chemist Raphael Liesegang” from its verb, “observed.”

C.why_wrong: The pair of commas treats “Raphael Liesegang” as extra information that could be removed, but without an article before “German chemist” the name is essential, so it should not be set off.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Liesegang rings: in 1896 the German chemist Raphael Eduard Liesegang saw silver nitrate dropped on gelatin containing potassium dichromate precipitate in concentric rings). Known history of chemistry. Band-7 checks: article-less descriptor + title + name used as the subject and followed at once by its verb (5aae2475 shape, 'plant cell biologist Yuree Lee showed'); full four-way menu (title, Name / title Name, / title, Name, / title Name); the comma pair looks polite. Section 6 exempts S4_restrictive from the cue-window check (local at every band).
band7_moves: title and name with a stacked descriptor (German chemist) used as the subject, followed at once by its verb, so a closing comma after the name looks natural
commas-around-the-name option (title, Name,), the band-7 decoy that looks polite

band7.why: nationality plus occupation title with the name as subject and the verb right after it, full four-way menu with the polite comma pair, same construction as 5aae2475 (plant cell biologist Yuree Lee showed); local by nature, as section 6 notes

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that clause
items.passage: Among the Fang peoples of Gabon, Cameroon, and Equatorial Guinea, the word mvet designates both a stringed ______ that musicians pluck while singing and the lengthy epics they perform to its accompaniment, which recount struggles between mortal clans and the immortals of Engong.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “that musicians pluck while singing” is restrictive: it identifies which stringed instrument the word mvet names. A restrictive clause is not set off from the noun it modifies, so no punctuation belongs between “instrument” and “that.”

B.why_wrong: A comma before “that” treats the restrictive clause “that musicians pluck while singing” as nonessential; a clause beginning with “that” is never set off this way.

C.why_wrong: A single dash has no partner and no role here; it cuts the noun “instrument” off from the clause “that musicians pluck while singing” that identifies it.

D.why_wrong: “And” has nothing to join: “that musicians pluck while singing” is not a second item parallel to “a stringed instrument,” so the sentence becomes ungrammatical (and the pairing “both ... and” is broken).

items.notes: Subject: literature and music (mvet, the harp-zither of the Fang, or Ekang, peoples of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, and the epic narratives of mortals and the immortals of Engong performed with it). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape and menu of 603755a5 (club / club, / club plus dash / club, and): a restrictive that clause after a long run in which a comma before the that clause looks natural; the following “and the lengthy epics” completes both ... and, which the and option breaks.

band7.why: restrictive that clause after a long run, 603755a5 band-6 menu with dash and comma-and decoys; band_target 6

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a list that specifies it
items.passage: In 1944, French archaeologist Louis Malleret began excavating Oc Eo, a port of the ancient kingdom of Funan in present-day southern Vietnam, and unearthed objects from across a vast trading ______ Indian seals and beads, fragments of Chinese bronze mirrors, and a gold medallion depicting the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the blank form a complete main clause (“Louis Malleret began excavating Oc Eo ... and unearthed objects from across a vast trading network”), and the words after it are a list that specifies those objects. A colon is the conventional mark to introduce such a list after a complete clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “Indian seals and beads, fragments of Chinese bronze mirrors, and a gold medallion ...” is only a list of noun phrases.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Indian seals and beads, fragments of Chinese bronze mirrors, and a gold medallion depicting the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “network Indian seals and beads” runs the list into the clause, and nothing signals that the list specifies the objects.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Oc Eo, Funan port in the Mekong Delta; Louis Malleret's 1944 excavation found Indian seals and beads, Han Chinese mirror fragments and a gold Roman medallion of Antoninus Pius). Known facts. Band-6 shape and single-mark menu of c468db1c: a long one-sentence run with an appositive and compound predicate before the announcing noun; period and semicolon both leave a fragment; no lone-dash option beside the colon key.

band7.why: colon before a list after a long clause with an appositive and compound predicate; c468db1c single-mark band-6 menu

items.subtype: Colon before a noun phrase that holds a relative clause with a finite verb
items.passage: The earliest known writing, which emerged in Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE, was used mainly to keep economic records. Archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat traces its origins to an unlikely ______ clay tokens that communities across the ancient Near East shaped into cones, disks, spheres, and cylinders and used for millennia to tally agricultural commodities such as grain, oil, and livestock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the blank form a complete main clause (“Archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat traces its origins to an unlikely source”), and what follows is a long noun phrase, “small clay tokens that communities across the ancient Near East shaped into cones, disks, spheres, and cylinders and used for millennia ...,” that names the source. A colon correctly introduces that explanation.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “small clay tokens that communities ... shaped ... and used for millennia ...” is a noun phrase: “shaped” and “used” belong to a relative clause that describes the tokens, so there is no main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Small clay tokens that communities across the ancient Near East shaped ... and used ...” a sentence of its own, but its only verbs are inside the relative clause that describes the tokens, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Adding “they were” makes the noun phrase a second main clause, “they were small clay tokens ...,” joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Denise Schmandt-Besserat's account of clay counting tokens in the ancient Near East as the precursor of writing; her well-known thesis, stated only as hers). Band-7 checks: announcing noun (an unlikely source) followed by a noun phrase holding a relative clause with two finite verbs and a series (that communities ... shaped into cones, disks, spheres, and cylinders and used ...), so semicolon and period options look right until the phrase is seen to lack a main verb (section 3 point 8); the decisive evidence (no main verb) runs to the end of the 39-word run; a context sentence first (proto-cuneiform tablets of about 3200 BCE were mainly administrative records); menu of e9aee0d8 (colon, semicolon, period, comma plus added words).
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon holds a relative clause with two finite verbs (that communities ... shaped ... and used ...), so the semicolon and period versions look like clause joints
added-words option (, they were small) turns the phrase into a spliced clause
the evidence against the strong marks sits 15 to 30 words past the blank

band7.why: noun phrase after the colon holds a relative clause with two finite verbs and a series, so semicolon and period look like clause joints until the end of the run; e9aee0d8 menu with the added-words splice

items.subtype: Closing dash of a pair around a long supplement between subject and verb
items.passage: In 1949, eleven long stone slabs were found in the village of Ndut Lieng Krak in Vietnam’s Central Highlands. The slabs—each flaked by prehistoric toolmakers into an elongated blade that produces a distinct tone when ______ are now considered among the oldest surviving lithophones, percussion instruments made of tuned stone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “The slabs” opens a supplementary element, “each flaked by prehistoric toolmakers into an elongated blade that produces a distinct tone when struck,” that comes between the subject “The slabs” and its verb “are.” A second dash after “struck” closes that element, so the subject links cleanly to “are now considered.”

B.why_wrong: An element opened with a dash must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

C.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the supplementary element opened after “The slabs” never ends, and “when struck are now considered” runs the element into the main verb.

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot close an element opened with a dash, and a colon between the subject “The slabs” and its verb “are” is not conventional.

items.notes: Subject: arts and archaeology (the Ndut Lieng Krak lithophone, eleven prehistoric stone slabs found in 1949 in Vietnam's Central Highlands, now among the oldest known stone instruments). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape of aacddbd8: the opening dash sits 21 words before the blank inside a second sentence, the element holds a relative clause and a when clause, and the subject's verb arrives right after the blank. Menu: dash key, comma (mismatched pair), no mark, colon.

band7.why: dash pair partner 21 words back, element holds a relative and a when clause; aacddbd8 band-6 shape, no nested level

items.subtype: Comma plus and between independent clauses, clause 2 opening with a long phrase
items.passage: The Spillings hoard, the largest cache of Viking Age silver ever discovered, was concealed beneath the floor of a farm building on the Swedish island of ______ for more than eleven centuries, its armbands, ingots, and thousands of coins, predominantly minted in the Islamic world, remained undisturbed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are main clauses: “The Spillings hoard ... was concealed beneath the floor of a farm building on the Swedish island of Gotland” and “for more than eleven centuries, its armbands, ingots, and thousands of coins ... remained undisturbed.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins two main clauses.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; reading “for more than eleven centuries” as part of the first clause does not help, because “its armbands, ingots, and thousands of coins ... remained undisturbed” is still a main clause joined by only a comma.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long main clauses like these, a comma goes before it.

C.why_wrong: With no mark and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together; “for more than eleven centuries” then seems to belong to the first clause, and the second clause starts without any boundary.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Spillings hoard, Gotland, the largest Viking Age silver hoard found, hidden about 870 and found in 1999; arm rings, ingots and some 14,000 coins, mostly Islamic dirhams). Known facts, figures rounded down. Band-6 shape of 59094d87: clause 2 opens with a 6-word time phrase that also reads naturally at the end of clause 1 (concealed ... for more than eleven centuries), and clause 2's subject carries its own series and a comma-set participial phrase before the verb, so the splice is 21 words past the blank. S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials (plan band 6).

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 (time phrase that attaches to either clause, splice 21 words past the blank)

items.subtype: No punctuation before and joining two noun clauses
items.passage: In 1891, American astronomer Seth Carlo Chandler reported that Earth’s rotational axis drifts in a small loop, completing a circuit approximately every 433 days. Geophysicists have since sought to explain what keeps this wobble from fading ______ and why its amplitude varies from one decade to the next.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “explain” has two objects joined by “and”: “what keeps this wobble from fading away” and “why its amplitude varies from one decade to the next.” Two elements of a compound joined by “and” are not separated by punctuation, so no mark belongs after “away.”

A.why_wrong: A comma before “and” would set off the second object of “explain,” but “and why its amplitude varies ...” is not a main clause; it is the second part of a compound object, so no comma is needed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “and why its amplitude varies from one decade to the next” is not a main clause; it is the second object of “explain.”

D.why_wrong: A colon would wrongly signal that what follows explains or specifies the first object, but “and why its amplitude varies ...” is simply a second, parallel object of “explain.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Chandler wobble: in 1891 Seth Carlo Chandler reported the roughly 433-day wobble of Earth's rotation axis; its continued excitation and its changing amplitude are long-studied problems). Known facts. Band-6 shape and menu of 6ea8c23f (regions, / regions: / regions; / regions): two noun clauses joined by and after a long run, where a comma before and looks natural. S4_compound has no band-7 officials (plan band 6).

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; band 6 like 6ea8c23f (two noun-clause objects joined by and after a long run)

items.subtype: Comma plus but between independent clauses
items.passage: The American paddlefish, a filter feeder native to the Mississippi River basin, has a long, paddle-shaped rostrum. Early naturalists assumed that the fish used it to dig up riverbed ______ researchers have since discovered that the rostrum is covered with thousands of receptors that detect the faint electrical signals given off by plankton.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are main clauses: “Early naturalists assumed that the fish used it to dig up riverbed mud” and “researchers have since discovered that the rostrum is covered with thousands of receptors ....” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast between the old assumption and the later discovery.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses “Early naturalists assumed ...” and “researchers have since discovered ....”

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses run together after “mud.”

D.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long main clauses like these, a comma goes before it.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (American paddlefish, Polyodon spathula: its rostrum carries thousands of electroreceptors that sense the weak electric fields of zooplankton; earlier ideas cast it as a digging tool). Known biology, no names. Medium shape: the subordinate that clause inside clause 1 (that the fish used it to dig up riverbed mud) makes the comma-only version feel like a continuing list; the second clause's subject is two words past the blank. Menu of 2.12 (skeptical but / skeptical, but / skeptical, / skeptical).

items.subtype: Comma plus and between independent clauses
items.passage: The Hikayat Hang Tuah, a Malay epic set largely in the fifteenth-century sultanate of Melaka, celebrates a warrior renowned for his loyalty. In its most famous episode, Hang Tuah kills his closest friend, Hang Jebat, for rebelling against the ______ generations of Malaysian readers have debated which of the two men is the story’s true hero.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are main clauses: “In its most famous episode, Hang Tuah kills his closest friend, Hang Jebat, for rebelling against the sultan” and “generations of Malaysian readers have debated which of the two men is the story’s true hero.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long main clauses like these, a comma goes before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the main clauses “Hang Tuah kills his closest friend ...” and “generations of Malaysian readers have debated ....”

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together after “sultan.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Hikayat Hang Tuah, Malay epic of Melaka; Tuah kills Jebat, who rebelled against the sultan, and Malaysian readers and critics have long argued over which of them is the real hero). Known facts. Medium shape of 2.5: the first clause carries an introductory phrase and an appositive comma pair, so a lone comma at the blank looks like part of the same rhythm; clause 2 opens with its subject. Menu of 2.5 (apiary, / apiary, and / apiary and / apiary).

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a participial phrase between subject and verb
items.passage: The birch-bark scrolls from ancient Gandhara that the British Library acquired in 1994, composed in the Gandhari language and written in a script called ______ are among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts ever discovered, dating approximately to the first century CE.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “acquired in 1994” opens a supplementary phrase, “composed in the Gandhari language and written in a script called Kharosthi,” that comes between the subject “The birch-bark scrolls from ancient Gandhara that the British Library acquired in 1994” and its verb “are.” A second comma after “Kharosthi” closes that phrase.

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the phrase opened after “acquired in 1994” never ends, and “a script called Kharosthi are among the oldest ...” runs the phrase into the main verb.

C.why_wrong: A phrase opened with a comma must be closed with a comma, not a dash.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “The birch-bark scrolls ... that the British Library acquired in 1994” from its verb “are,” and neither side is a complete main clause.

items.notes: Subject: history and religion (the British Library's Gandharan Buddhist scrolls, acquired 1994, birch bark, Gandhari language in Kharosthi script, about the first century CE). Known facts. Medium shape: a long subject with a restrictive that clause, then a comma-set participial phrase holding its own and; the opening comma sits 13 words before the blank, so a student must look back to find the partner (2.14, 2.6).

fixes: why_wrong for D quoted the subject as “The scrolls”; now quotes the passage word for word

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Samoans regard the palolo, a marine worm that lives burrowed inside coral reefs for most of the year, as a seasonal delicacy. On one or two nights each October or November, these worms simultaneously detach their reproductive segments, which ascend to the surface before ______ the surrounding water with eggs and sperm.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “these worms simultaneously detach their reproductive segments, which ascend to the surface before dawn” is followed by the participial phrase “clouding the surrounding water with eggs and sperm,” which describes what the rising segments do. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “Clouding the surrounding water with eggs and sperm” a sentence of its own, but it has no subject and no main verb, so it is a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “clouding the surrounding water with eggs and sperm” is a participial phrase, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: With no comma, “before dawn clouding the surrounding water” makes the phrase seem to describe the dawn; a comma is needed to set off the phrase that describes the rising segments.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (palolo worm, Palola viridis, of Samoa and other Pacific reefs: on one or two nights in October or November its reproductive rear segments break off and swarm to the surface before dawn, releasing gametes; Samoans harvest them as a delicacy). Known biology, no names. Medium shape and menu of 2.26 (fungi; producing / fungi. Producing / fungi producing / fungi, producing): the participial tail could be misread as describing the noun before it (dawn), as 2.26's can (fungi producing ... paintings). Replaces the claimed mangrove killifish, a twin of live transitions w1b2_16.

items.subtype: Closing dash of a pair around an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: In 1832, Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau introduced the phenakistiscope, an early device for creating the illusion of motion. Its principal component—a cardboard disk printed with a sequence of drawings and perforated with narrow slits around its ______ was rotated in front of a mirror while the viewer peered through the slits at the reflected images.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “Its principal component” opens a supplementary element, “a cardboard disk printed with a sequence of drawings and perforated with narrow slits around its edge,” that describes the component and comes between the subject and its verb, “was rotated.” A second dash after “edge” closes that element.

A.why_wrong: An element opened with a dash must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

B.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the element opened after “Its principal component” never ends, and “around its edge was rotated” runs the element into the main verb.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “Its principal component” from its verb “was rotated,” and neither side is a complete main clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts and technology (Joseph Plateau's phenakistiscope of 1832, a slotted, drawn cardboard disk spun before a mirror). Known history. Medium shape and menu of 2.13 (prose; / prose / prose, / prose plus dash): the opening dash sits 16 words before the blank, the appositive holds its own and, and the verb follows the blank.

items.subtype: Comma after a long introductory participial phrase
items.passage: First identified in 1868 by Swedish physicist Anders Ångström, a founder of the science of ______ the faint glow known as airglow, which is given off by atoms and molecules high in the atmosphere, keeps the night sky from ever being completely dark.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the participial phrase “First identified in 1868 by Swedish physicist Anders Ångström, a founder of the science of spectroscopy,” which describes the subject that follows, “the faint glow known as airglow.” A comma correctly separates this introductory phrase from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “First identified in 1868 by Swedish physicist Anders Ångström, a founder of the science of spectroscopy” is only an introductory phrase.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the words before the blank are an introductory phrase, not a main clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the subject, so “the science of spectroscopy the faint glow” reads as one confused string.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (airglow, the faint light given off by the upper atmosphere that keeps the night sky from being completely dark, first identified in 1868 by Anders Ångström, one of the founders of spectroscopy; both facts as stated in Wikipedia, Airglow and Anders Jonas Ångström). Review replaced Earth's hum, which is live in text_structure_and_purpose w4b1_07. Medium shape of 2.20 and 2.25: a 16-word participial opener with an appositive that ends on a plain noun, so the noun phrase after the blank can briefly read as a second appositive until the verb “keeps”; a long subject with a restrictive participle and a which clause before the verb. Menu of 2.25 (world / world: / world; / world,).

fixes: replaced the subject: Earth's hum is live in text_structure_and_purpose w4b1_07 (seismic hum, ocean waves on the seafloor); new subject airglow (grepped, claimed), same S2_intro_comma menu and key D; explanation and why_wrong rewritten

items.subtype: No punctuation before and joining two how clauses
items.passage: The Diderot effect, the tendency for one new acquisition to trigger a cascade of others, is named for a 1769 essay by French philosopher Denis Diderot. In it, Diderot describes how a luxurious dressing gown made his old furnishings look ______ how he replaced one possession after another until his study no longer felt like his own.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “describes” has two objects joined by “and”: “how a luxurious dressing gown made his old furnishings look shabby” and “how he replaced one possession after another ....” The two parts of a compound joined by “and” are not separated by punctuation.

B.why_wrong: A comma before “and” would set off the second object of “describes,” but “how he replaced one possession after another ...” is not a main clause; it is the second part of a compound object, so no comma is needed.

C.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit; comma after the conjunction
C.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “and” split the compound object and also separate “and” from the clause it introduces.

D.why_wrong: A comma after “and” separates the conjunction from “how he replaced ...,” the clause it joins to the first object.

items.notes: Subject: social science and philosophy (Diderot effect, named for Diderot's essay 'Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown,' usually dated 1769; the term was later coined by anthropologist Grant McCracken). Known facts. Medium shape of 2.23: a compound of two clauses joined by and after a long first element, where a comma before and feels natural; options vary only commas around and, as in 2.23.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Al Sadu is a weaving tradition practiced by Bedouin women in the Arabian Peninsula. Working on ground looms, weavers turn fibers ______ sheep, camels, and goats into tent walls, rugs, and saddlebags decorated with bold geometric patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The preposition “from” and its object, “sheep, camels, and goats,” form one phrase that tells where the fibers come from. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “weavers turn fibers from” is not complete; the colon splits the preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A single dash has no role here; it separates the preposition “from” from its object, “sheep, camels, and goats.”

D.why_wrong: A comma separates the preposition “from” from its object, which is not conventional.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Al Sadu, Bedouin women's weaving of sheep wool, camel hair and goat hair on ground looms for tents, rugs and camel trappings, Arabian Peninsula). Known facts, no names. Easy shape of 1.5 and 1.9: a context sentence, then the blank between a preposition and a series that is its object; four different marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Boulengerula taitanus is a limbless, burrowing amphibian found in the Taita Hills of southeastern Kenya. Soon after they hatch, its young feed ______ their mother’s skin, using specialized teeth to peel off its fatty, nutrient-rich outer layer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “feed on their mother’s skin,” the preposition “on” and its object, “their mother’s skin,” belong together. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A single dash has no role here; it separates the preposition “on” from its object, “their mother’s skin.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause, but “its young feed on” is not complete without the object of “on.”

C.why_wrong: A comma separates the preposition “on” from its object, which is not conventional.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Boulengerula taitanus, a caecilian of the Taita Hills, Kenya: mothers grow a thick, lipid-rich outer skin that the young peel off and eat with specialized teeth, reported in 2006). Known biology, no names. Easy shape of 1.21 and 1.23 (embodied by, home to): verb plus preposition, blank before the preposition's object.

items.subtype: Direct question after a colon: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: Some early Greek inscriptions are written in boustrophedon, a style in which the direction of writing reverses at the end of every line, like an ox plowing a field. This style raises a question that historians still discuss: Why ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words after the colon, beginning with “Why,” ask a direct question. A direct question uses inverted word order (“did scribes choose”) and ends with a question mark.

A.recipe: question errors (period on a direct question)
A.why_wrong: The word order is correct for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.why_wrong: A direct question needs inverted order, with the helping verb “did” before the subject; “Why scribes chose this method?” keeps statement order.

D.why_wrong: “Why scribes chose this method.” uses statement order and a period, but the colon introduces the question itself, which must be asked directly.

items.notes: Subject: language and writing (boustrophedon, ox-turning writing in early Greek inscriptions). Known facts. Easy shape of 1.18: a context sentence, then a direct question introduced by a colon, blank ending the passage; full 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark.

items.subtype: Comma plus but between independent clauses
items.passage: Market researchers often ask consumers whether they intend to buy a product in order to forecast ______ simply answering such a question can make people more likely to buy, a pattern known as the mere-measurement effect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are main clauses: “Market researchers often ask consumers whether they intend to buy a product in order to forecast sales” and “simply answering such a question can make people more likely to buy.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two long main clauses like these, a comma goes before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together after “sales.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (mere-measurement effect: asking about purchase intentions raises later purchase rates). Known finding, no names. Easy shape and menu of 1.2 (fibers, / fibers but / fibers / fibers, but): one sentence, the second clause opens with its gerund subject right after the blank, and a sentence appositive closes it.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: A tughra is an elaborate calligraphic emblem that served as the official signature of an Ottoman sultan. When a new sultan rose to the ______ court calligraphers designed a tughra combining his name with his father’s, and it appeared on decrees, coins, and even the walls of buildings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause “When a new sultan rose to the throne,” which must be followed by a main clause, “court calligraphers designed a tughra combining his name with his father’s.” A comma correctly separates the introductory dependent clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: The period makes “When a new sultan rose to the throne” a sentence of its own, but a clause beginning with “When” cannot stand alone, so it is a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “When a new sultan rose to the throne” is a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs straight into the main clause, so “rose to the throne court calligraphers” reads as one confused string.

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (tughra, the calligraphic monogram made for each Ottoman sultan on accession, with his name and his father's, used on decrees, coins and buildings). Known facts. Easy shape of 1.6 and 1.8 (Because ..., Although ...): a context sentence, then an introductory When clause ending at the blank before the main clause's subject; menu of 1.19 (classroom. / classroom; / classroom, / classroom). Varied from item 17, whose opener is a participle.

items.subtype: Restrictive that clause: no comma, and the that is needed
items.passage: Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth dozens of times every second. In 1952, German physicist Winfried Otto Schumann predicted that these strikes would produce low-frequency radio ______ bounce back and forth between the ground and the ionosphere, a layer of charged particles high in the atmosphere.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “that bounce back and forth between the ground and the ionosphere” identifies which low-frequency radio waves Schumann predicted. A restrictive clause like this one begins with “that” and is not set off from the noun it modifies with a comma.

A.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “bounce” has no link to “waves,” so the sentence reads “these strikes would produce low-frequency radio waves, bounce back and forth ...,” which is not grammatical.

C.why_wrong: Without “that,” “radio waves bounce back and forth” is a clause dropped into the sentence with no connection to “would produce,” so the sentence is not grammatical.

D.why_wrong: A comma before “that” treats the restrictive clause as nonessential; a clause beginning with “that” is not set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Schumann resonances: in 1952 Winfried Otto Schumann predicted lightning-excited extremely low-frequency waves resonating in the cavity between the ground and the ionosphere; lightning strikes Earth roughly 40 to 50 times a second). Known physics. Easy shape and menu of 1.29 (company, / company that / company / company, that).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses, the second opening with its subject
items.passage: Radiolarians are single-celled organisms that drift through the world’s oceans as part of the plankton. Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of ______ skeletons often take the shape of spheres, spirals, or spiky stars, and many are barely visible to the naked eye.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of silica” is a main clause, and “These skeletons often take the shape of spheres, spirals, or spiky stars, and many are barely visible to the naked eye” is another. A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses “Each one builds an intricate skeleton out of silica” and “these skeletons often take the shape ....”

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together after “silica.”

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses like these, a comma goes before it; without one, the clauses are not correctly joined.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (radiolarians, single-celled marine plankton with ornate silica skeletons). Known biology, no names. Easy shape and menu of 1.14 (settings she / settings, she / settings and she / settings. She): the second clause opens with its subject right after the blank.
